name: Sodium hyaluronate
lead: Sodium hyaluronate is the sodium salt of hyaluronic acid (HA, also called hyaluronan), a long chain sugar polymer made of repeating glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine units that occurs naturally in skin, joint fluid and the eye [1][2][3]. It is the form most often listed on moisturiser and serum labels, where it is used to make skin look and feel more hydrated, smoother and plumper [1][3].

For appearance, people use it in two main ways. Topical products containing sodium hyaluronate act as humectants, drawing and holding water in the outer skin so that fine dry-skin lines look softer and the surface looks dewy; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as reaching deeper layers [1]. Cross-linked HA is also the base material of injectable dermal fillers used to add volume to lips, cheeks and the jawline and to soften facial wrinkles, with results that typically last about 6 to 12 months [3].

Outside cosmetics the same substance is used in medicine: knee and other joint injections, viscoelastic gels that protect the eye during cataract surgery, submucosal lifts in endoscopic resection, and dental and wound products [4][5][6][7][8][9]. Most published clinical trials come from these uses rather than from cosmetic creams.

paras: Hyaluronic acid is a non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan whose disaccharide units are joined by alternating beta-1,4 and beta-1,3 linkages. In the body its molecular weight ranges from a few thousand to around 20 million daltons, and chains can reach tens of thousands of repeating units [3]. Unlike other glycosaminoglycans it is made at the cell membrane rather than in the Golgi apparatus [3]. In salt form, with sodium as the counter-ion, it dissolves readily in water, which is why it is the usual choice for formulations [1].

In skin, HA is abundant in the basal epidermis where keratinocytes divide, and it helps keep the extracellular space open and hydrated [3]. Reviews describe it as taking part in keratinocyte proliferation and migration during re-epithelialisation, and its main receptor in the epidermis is CD44 [3]. After heavy UVB exposure, skin cells are reported to make less HA and break it down faster [3]. Synovial fluid contains HA at high molecular weight, and a 1985 study measured how its concentration and molecular weight differ in rheumatoid arthritis and other joint diseases [2][12].

Sodium hyaluronate is listed in moisturisers, serums, masks and eye creams, and the European CosIng database records skin-conditioning and humectant functions for hyaluronic acid [1][3]. Brands commonly combine several molecular weights in one product: larger chains are described as forming a hydrating film on the surface, while smaller fragments are described as moving into the upper skin [1].

Cross-linked HA gels are a separate category. They are injected by clinicians as dermal fillers to smooth facial wrinkles and add volume, and the effect lasts about 6 to 12 months before the body gradually breaks the gel down [3]. The US FDA has approved HA fillers for facial wrinkle use [3].

Sodium hyaluronate products are used for knee osteoarthritis injections [4][5], as viscoelastic agents in cataract surgery [6][7], and as a submucosal lift in endoscopic resection [8][9]. Studies have also examined a sodium hyaluronate and carboxymethylcellulose membrane for preventing postoperative abdominal adhesions [10], injections for shoulder, jaw and tendon conditions [17], and HA gels as dressings after gum graft harvesting.

With injectable fillers, reported complications include pain, bruising, redness and itching, injury to nerves or small vessels, vascular occlusion, and occasional granulomatous foreign-body reactions [3]. Topical use is generally described as well tolerated, with irritation or allergy possible with any cosmetic ingredient; a Grokipedia summary states hypersensitivity and infection are rare [1]. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review programme published a safety assessment covering hyaluronic acid, potassium hyaluronate and sodium hyaluronate in 2009 [18]. A 2012 review noted possible adverse effects of intra-articular HA injections [3].

Karl Meyer and John Palmer first isolated hyaluronic acid from the vitreous of cow eyes in 1934, naming it from the Greek hyalos, meaning glassy [3]. Commercial extraction later used pig skin and rooster combs, and bacterial fermentation, including modified Bacillus strains, now supplies much of the material [3]. In the 1970s and 1980s Pharmacia developed Healon, the first HA biomedical product, for eye surgery, when intraocular lens implants created a need for a viscous protective lubricant [3]. Manufacturers then cross-linked or chemically stabilised HA to extend its short half-life in tissue, which made injectable fillers possible [3]. A 1985 Science paper reported that partial degradation fragments of HA, but not intact or fully digested material, induced new blood vessel formation in a chick membrane assay [11].

Hyaluronic acid serums became one of the most widely stocked categories in mainstream skincare, and the ingredient is a staple of routine-building discussions among people improving their skin. Fillers made from it are among the most common minimally invasive cosmetic procedures. Product names and marketing claims about molecular weight and depth of penetration vary by brand [1].

Most trials involve medical rather than cosmetic uses. A 1998 randomized trial of intra-articular sodium hyaluronate (Hyalgan) in knee osteoarthritis was reported by the Hyalgan Study Group [4], and a registered trial with 421 participants compared two brands for knee osteoarthritis [5]. A 2022 systematic review of 38 randomized trials examined HA injections for knee osteoarthritis and reported ongoing questions about the number of injections, preparation type and duration of effect [19]. Registered trials also cover shoulder, ankle and hip osteoarthritis [13][14][15], tennis elbow [16], and cataract surgery viscoelastics [6][7]. A 2010 Lancet systematic review examined injections including hyaluronate for tendinopathy [17].

Related reviews: a 2023 Cochrane review of HA dressings for chronic wounds included 12 trials with 1,108 participants [20], and a 2023 rapid evidence review described the evidence for hyaluronate injections in temporomandibular disorders as weak [21]. A 2024 randomized trial examined a gel containing sodium hyaluronate on gum graft donor sites [22]. No trial of topical sodium hyaluronate for facial appearance was found.

card.summary: The salt form of hyaluronic acid in most moisturisers and serums; well established medically, with little direct data on topical looks effects.
card.note: Strong evidence base is for injections and surgery, not facial creams.

quick.overview:
Sodium hyaluronate is the common salt form of hyaluronic acid, a water-binding molecule naturally present in skin and joints. It appears in many moisturisers and serums.

Most clinical research concerns joint injections and eye surgery rather than cosmetic creams.
quick.mechanism: It is a humectant that binds water; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as penetrating deeper.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally described as well tolerated. Injectable forms (fillers) carry reported risks such as bruising, vascular occlusion and granulomas.

chain: Binds water at the skin surface
Skin looks more hydrated and plump
Fine dryness lines look softer; skin appears smoother
angle.text: Applied in a moisturiser or serum, sodium hyaluronate holds water at the skin surface, which makes dry skin look smoother and more supple while it is in place. In injectable filler form, cross-linked HA adds volume under the skin to reshape lips, cheeks and folds.
